mcqs.question: A function reads a global mutable counter and returns it without modifying anything. Is it pure?
options: Yes, because it has no side effects
No, because purity requires the function to take at least one argument
No, because its output depends on state outside its arguments, so the same call can return different results over time
Yes, as long as the counter is never negative
mcqs.explanation: Purity needs both determinism and no side effects. Reading a mutable global breaks determinism even without writing anything — the same call can answer differently later, which is exactly what referential transparency rules out. Argument count is irrelevant.

mcqs.question: After calling an impure function that mutates a shared list argument in place, what happens to other code holding a reference to that same list?
options: Nothing changes unless that code also calls the function again
It sees a compile error the next time it accesses the list
It automatically receives an immutable snapshot from before the call
It sees the mutated version immediately, even though it never called the function itself
mcqs.explanation: In-place mutation changes the one object every reference points at, so any other holder of that reference observes the change immediately and unexpectedly. Returning a new list instead of mutating avoids this exact surprise, at the cost of an allocation.

mcqs.question: Why does immutability reduce the need for locks in concurrent code?
options: It makes every operation run in constant time regardless of thread count
A race condition needs shared state plus a writer; removing the writer removes the race even with shared reads
Immutable values are automatically stored in thread-local memory
It replaces locks with automatic retries on conflict
mcqs.explanation: Races come from concurrent writes to shared state. If a value can never change after creation, concurrent readers can't observe a half-updated value and there's nothing to synchronize on. It doesn't touch time complexity or storage location, and it isn't a retry mechanism.

mcqs.question: A function computes a deterministic result but also calls a logger with `log.info(...)` before returning. Is it pure?
options: Yes, logging doesn't count as a side effect if the return value is deterministic
No, because writing to the log stream is an observable side effect, even though the return value is deterministic
Yes, as long as the log call happens after the computation, not before
No, but only if the log level is set to a value that actually writes output
mcqs.explanation: Purity requires zero observable side effects, and writing to a log stream is observable — it changes something outside the function's return value. Determinism of the return value is necessary but not sufficient; the ordering of the log call and whether output is actually written don't change that a side effect occurred.

mcqs.question: Compared to mutating a list in place, what does the functional "return a new list" approach typically cost, and what does it buy?
options: It costs nothing extra and buys nothing extra — the two are equivalent at runtime
It costs extra time complexity (O(n log n) instead of O(n)) in exchange for thread safety
It costs extra memory for the new structure, in exchange for the old value staying valid and no other reference being surprised
It costs extra memory but makes the operation impossible to test
mcqs.explanation: Filtering into a new list is still O(n) time; the real trade is O(n) extra space for the new structure, bought in exchange for leaving the original untouched — no aliasing surprises and the old version stays usable for undo or comparison. It has no bearing on testability, and it doesn't change the time complexity class.
